what_this_is: The catalogue of MySQL stored-program (SQL/PSM) constructs Phase 4b recognises, in the same row shape as constructs.json. There is no deterministic MySQL -> PL/pgSQL converter, so nothing here is tier 'rule': every routine goes to the reasoning tier and then through the same five gates as Oracle code. `marker` is what parity requires in the converted text when a construct is claimed translated; `residue: true` means the MySQL form must be gone from the output. Written against the seven routines of DBMIG_MYSQL_APP on 2026-09-29. Tiers: model = needs judgement; manual = no PostgreSQL equivalent, a person's decision.

constructs.name: backtick-quoted identifier
constructs.postgres: unquoted lower-case name (double quotes only where unavoidable)
constructs.note: Backticks are a syntax error in PostgreSQL. Names are lower-case on the target, so they are simply unquoted; a reserved word was renamed by Phase 4c (a table `order` is `order_tbl`).

constructs.name: DEFINER= clause
constructs.note: MySQL routines run with the definer's rights by default; PostgreSQL functions run with the caller's. SECURITY DEFINER is never added by a conversion -- if a caller relied on the definer's privileges, record it as not_translated with the reason.

constructs.name: READS/MODIFIES SQL DATA
constructs.note: MySQL's data-access characteristic is advisory. A function that reads tables is at most STABLE; one that writes is VOLATILE.

constructs.name: DETERMINISTIC
constructs.postgres: IMMUTABLE only for a function that reads no tables; otherwise STABLE
constructs.note: MySQL never checks DETERMINISTIC. fn_customer_balance declares it but reads customer_order and payment: marking it IMMUTABLE would let PostgreSQL cache a stale balance. Only a pure function (fn_legacy_tax_rate) may be IMMUTABLE.

constructs.name: CHARSET on a return type
constructs.note: PostgreSQL has one encoding per database.

constructs.name: UNSIGNED parameter or variable
constructs.postgres: the widened type Phase 4c uses (int unsigned -> bigint, bigint unsigned key -> bigint)
constructs.note: PostgreSQL has no unsigned types. A parameter that relied on the type to refuse negatives needs an explicit check (SCT 8850).

constructs.name: SELECT ... INTO variable
constructs.postgres: SELECT ... INTO (NOT STRICT where the code tests the variable for NULL afterwards)
constructs.note: NOT the Oracle rule. MySQL leaves the variable unchanged (NULL if fresh) on zero rows and errors on more than one; PL/pgSQL without STRICT sets NULL on zero rows and silently takes the first of many; with STRICT it raises on both. sp_place_order tests IF v_customer_id IS NULL right after its SELECT INTO, so STRICT would turn that check into an unhandled exception. Keep non-STRICT where the code handles NULL, and say in the note what happens on more than one row.

constructs.name: IFNULL()
constructs.note: Same two-argument semantics.

constructs.name: GROUP_CONCAT()
constructs.note: Separator and ORDER BY move inside string_agg. MySQL silently truncates the result at group_concat_max_len (1024 bytes by default); string_agg does not, so a longer list appears on the target that never appeared on the source.

constructs.name: CONCAT()
constructs.note: MySQL CONCAT() returns NULL if any argument is NULL. PostgreSQL concat() skips NULLs; || propagates them like MySQL. Use || unless skipping NULLs is intended.

constructs.name: DATE_FORMAT()
constructs.note: The format mask is translated: %Y -> YYYY, %m -> MM, %d -> DD, %H -> HH24, %i -> MI, %s -> SS.

constructs.name: NOW()
constructs.note: MySQL NOW() is a zone-less DATETIME in the session zone; PostgreSQL now() is timestamptz. Into a timestamp column, LOCALTIMESTAMP is the exact counterpart.

constructs.name: YEAR()
constructs.note: EXTRACT returns numeric; cast where an integer column receives it.

constructs.name: RAND()
constructs.note: Same [0,1) range.

constructs.name: CURRENT_USER()
constructs.note: Different VALUE, not just syntax: MySQL returns 'user@host', PostgreSQL the role name. An audit column that stored user@host will hold a different string after cutover.

constructs.name: LAST_INSERT_ID()
constructs.note: RETURNING reads the key of the row just inserted, which is what LAST_INSERT_ID() was being used for.

constructs.name: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE
constructs.postgres: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (<key columns>) DO UPDATE SET col = t.col + EXCLUDED.col
constructs.note: The conflict target must be named (SCT 8829). VALUES(col) becomes EXCLUDED.col, and the existing row's column is qualified with the table name or alias.

constructs.name: SIGNAL SQLSTATE
constructs.note: SQLSTATE '45000' is MySQL's user-defined-error state; PostgreSQL's is P0001 (raise_exception). Callers matching the MySQL error must change with it (SCT 8844).

constructs.name: RESIGNAL
constructs.note: A bare RAISE re-throws the caught error with its original SQLSTATE and message.

constructs.name: DECLARE EXIT HANDLER
constructs.note: An exception block in PL/pgSQL also rolls back everything the block did, so a handler whose only job was ROLLBACK becomes just the re-raise.

constructs.name: CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND
constructs.postgres: FETCH ...; EXIT WHEN NOT FOUND; (or a FOR rec IN query LOOP)
constructs.note: The flag-variable idiom (SET v_done = 1) is replaced by PL/pgSQL's FOUND.

constructs.name: CONTINUE HANDLER for an error
constructs.postgres: a BEGIN ... EXCEPTION block around each statement that may fail
constructs.note: PL/pgSQL cannot resume after an error at the next statement; each statement the handler covered needs its own block.

constructs.name: DECLARE ... CURSOR FOR
constructs.postgres: a FOR rec IN query LOOP, or a declared cursor
constructs.note: A FOR loop over the query is shorter and closes itself.

constructs.name: label: LOOP / LEAVE label
constructs.note: Labels move into << >>; LEAVE is EXIT and ITERATE is CONTINUE.

constructs.name: LIMIT offset, count
constructs.note: MySQL's two-argument LIMIT puts the offset first.

constructs.name: SET variable = expression
constructs.note: Assignment syntax. Not the SET of an UPDATE.

constructs.name: START TRANSACTION in a routine
constructs.postgres: removed -- the caller's transaction makes the work atomic
constructs.note: A PostgreSQL procedure may COMMIT only when CALLed outside a transaction, and never inside a block with an EXCEPTION clause -- which is exactly the shape an EXIT HANDLER converts to (SCT 8859). Remove START TRANSACTION / COMMIT / ROLLBACK and say so in the note; callers that relied on the routine committing now commit themselves.

constructs.name: COMMIT / ROLLBACK in a routine
constructs.postgres: removed, or COMMIT in a procedure with no EXCEPTION block
constructs.note: See START TRANSACTION. A function may never COMMIT; parity rejects one that does.

constructs.name: row-level trigger
constructs.note: A BEFORE trigger must RETURN NEW or the row change is silently cancelled; an AFTER trigger returns NULL. SET NEW.col = x becomes NEW.col := x.

constructs.name: PREPARE / EXECUTE dynamic SQL
constructs.note: Identifiers are quoted with format('%I'), values passed with USING -- never concatenated.

constructs.name: LOAD DATA / SELECT INTO OUTFILE
constructs.postgres: no in-database equivalent on RDS (aws_s3 import/export)
constructs.note: RDS has no server filesystem. Moving the file exchange to S3 is a design decision.

constructs.name: sys_exec / sys_eval
constructs.postgres: none -- shell execution is not available on RDS
constructs.note: An operating-system call from the database has no managed-service equivalent.
